title: Errors, MAC addresses and protocol state machines
summary: Returning several error types from one function: Box<dyn Error>, a custom error enum with Display, Error and From so ? converts automatically, and when unwrap is acceptable; trait objects in Rust in Action's role-playing game; MAC addresses as a newtype with local and multicast bits; and network protocols as enum state machines.

blocks.title: One function, several kinds of error
blocks.md: Network code fails in many ways: the address does not parse (`AddrParseError`), the connection is refused (`io::Error`), the reply is not a number (`ParseIntError`). A function that uses `?` on all three cannot return `Result<T, io::Error>`, because `?` only converts errors into the declared type. *Rust in Action* shows three ways out.

blocks.output:
error[E0277]: `?` couldn't convert the error to `std::io::Error`
 --> src/main.rs:7:47
  |
4 | fn main() -> Result<(), std::io::Error> {
  |              -------------------------- expected `std::io::Error` because of this
...
7 |     let _localhost = "::1".parse::<Ipv6Addr>()?;
  |                            -------------------^ the trait `From<AddrParseError>` is not implemented for `std::io::Error`
  |                            |
  |                            this can't be annotated with `?` because it has type `Result<_, AddrParseError>`
  |
  = note: the question mark operation (`?`) implicitly performs a conversion on the error value using the `From` trait
  = help: `std::io::Error` implements trait `From<T>`:
            From<ErrorKind>
            From<IntoInnerError<W>>
            From<NulError>
            From<TryReserveError>
            From<std::fs::TryLockError>
blocks.explain: `?` needs a `From<AddrParseError> for io::Error` impl to convert the error, and none exists.

blocks.title: Way 1: Box<dyn Error>
blocks.md: Every error type implements the `std::error::Error` trait, and there is a blanket `From<E: Error> for Box<dyn Error>`. So a function returning `Result<T, Box<dyn Error>>` can use `?` on anything. It is quick and fine for applications, but callers lose the concrete type: they can print the error, but matching on it needs `downcast_ref`.

blocks.output:
Ok((::1, 8080))
number too large to fit in target type
invalid IPv6 address syntax
is AddrParseError: true

blocks.title: Way 2: your own error type

blocks.output:
fix the address, please
I/O error: No such file or directory (os error 2) (source: true)
blocks.explain: The `?` operator calls `From::from` on the error, which is why the two `impl From` blocks are all it takes for both `?`s to compile. The `thiserror` crate generates exactly this boilerplate from attributes; `anyhow` is a richer `Box<dyn Error>` for applications.

blocks.title: Way 3: unwrap and expect
blocks.md: *Rust in Action* also lists "cheating" with `unwrap()` and `expect()`. In prototypes, examples and tests that is reasonable: a crash with a message is what you want. In library code it turns a recoverable error into a panic for every user, so prefer the error enum there.

blocks.title: Trait objects in a tiny game
blocks.md: *Rust in Action* introduces trait objects (chapter 18 of this course) with a role-playing game: dwarves, elves and humans can all `enchant` things, and a party is a `Vec<&dyn Enchanter>`. Different types, one interface, chosen at run time:

blocks.output:
Dwarf mutters incoherently. The Sword glows brightly.
Human mutters incoherently. The Sword fizzes, then turns into a worthless trinket.
Elf mutters incoherently. The Trinket glows brightly.

blocks.title: MAC addresses
blocks.md:
IP addresses route between networks; on the local network, Ethernet and Wi-Fi deliver **frames** to **MAC addresses**: 48 bits (6 bytes), written `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff`, normally burned in by the manufacturer. They are not hierarchical: numerically close addresses can be on different continents.

Two bits of the **first byte** carry meaning:

- bit 1 (`0b10`): **locally administered** if set, universal (assigned by the manufacturer under an IEEE prefix) if clear. Addresses you invent in software must set it.
- bit 0 (`0b01`): **multicast** (a group address) if set, **unicast** (one device) if clear.

*Rust in Action*'s `macgen` wraps the bytes in a newtype and sets both bits with `|=`. Note one detail: by the IEEE definition, setting bit 0 makes the address **multicast**; its `is_unicast` method actually tests the multicast bit. A generated unicast address should set bit 1 and **clear** bit 0, as below.

blocks.output:
mac: e6:e0:b7:36:8e:c1 local=true multicast=false
ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff local=true multicast=true

blocks.title: Protocols as state machines
blocks.md: A network connection moves through **states**: connecting, sending, waiting for a reply, closed. *Rust in Action* models this with an enum, a `loop` and a `match` that computes the next state. Because each state is a variant that can carry data, impossible combinations (a reply buffer while not yet connected) cannot be represented. The match makes every transition explicit, and the compiler checks that every state is handled.

blocks.title: An error type for a port scanner
blocks.md: `parse_target("host:port")` must return `Result<(String, u16), TargetError>`. Define `TargetError` with variants `MissingPort`, `BadPort(ParseIntError)` and `EmptyHost`, implement `Display` and `From<ParseIntError>`, and use `?` for the port.
blocks.task: Print `Ok(("example.com", 443))`, `missing :port`, `bad port: invalid digit found in string`, `empty host`.
blocks.expected_output:
Ok(("example.com", 443))
missing :port
bad port: invalid digit found in string
empty host
hints: With `impl From<ParseIntError> for TargetError`, `port.parse()?` converts the error for you.

blocks.title: A connection library
blocks.goal: Design a library error type that wraps several downstream errors, a MAC address type, and a connection state machine with checked transitions.
blocks.behavior:
Errors:
- `pub enum NetError { Io(io::Error), Addr(AddrParseError), Port(ParseIntError), Protocol(String) }` with `Display` (`"io: ..."`, `"address: ..."`, `"port: ..."`, `"protocol: ..."`), `std::error::Error` (with `source` returning the wrapped error for the first three) and `From` for the three wrapped types.
- `pub fn parse_endpoint(s: &str) -> Result<SocketAddr, NetError>`: `"IP:PORT"` for IPv4 only, split at the last `:`; uses `?` for both parts.
MAC:
- `pub struct Mac(pub [u8; 6])` with `Display` (lowercase, colon-separated), `pub fn parse(s: &str) -> Result<Mac, NetError>` (six two-digit hex groups separated by `:` or `-`; anything else is a `Protocol` error), `is_local`, `is_multicast`, and `pub fn local_unicast(bytes: [u8; 6]) -> Mac`.
State machine:
- `pub enum Conn { Closed, SynSent, Established { sent: usize, received: usize }, FinWait }` and `pub enum Event { Open, SynAck, Send(usize), Recv(usize), Close, Ack }`.
- `pub fn step(state: Conn, event: Event) -> Result<Conn, NetError>`: Closed + Open → SynSent; SynSent + SynAck → Established {0, 0}; Established + Send(n)/Recv(n) adds to the counters; Established + Close → FinWait; FinWait + Ack → Closed. Every other pair is `Protocol("<state> cannot handle <event>")` using the `Debug` names, e.g. `"Closed cannot handle Send(5)"`.

examples.output: Err(NetError::Port(..)), displayed as "port: invalid digit found in string"

hints: `parse_endpoint`: `let (ip, port) = s.rsplit_once(':').ok_or_else(|| NetError::Protocol(...))?; let ip: Ipv4Addr = ip.parse()?; let port: u16 = port.parse()?;`
Mac parsing: `s.split(|c| c == ':' || c == '-')`, check there are six parts of length 2, then `u8::from_str_radix(part, 16)`.
Derive `Debug` on `Conn` and `Event` so the error message can use `{:?}`; for the state name only, a small `fn name(&self) -> &'static str` helps.
blocks.solution_explain: With the three `From` impls, `?` turns `AddrParseError` and `ParseIntError` into `NetError` without any `map_err`. Matching on the pair `(state, event)` lists every legal transition in one place, and the final arm turns everything else into an error instead of a silent no-op.

questions.q: Why does `?` on an AddrParseError fail in a function returning `Result<T, io::Error>`?
options: There is no From<AddrParseError> for io::Error

questions.q: What is the drawback of returning `Box<dyn Error>` from a library?
options: Callers lose the concrete error type and must downcast to match on it

questions.q: What makes a custom error enum work smoothly with `?`?
questions.explanation: From does the conversion; Display and Error make it a proper error.

questions.q: Which bit of a MAC address's first byte marks a multicast address?
Why model a protocol as an enum state machine?
options: Each state carries only its own data and match forces every transition to be handled

points: `?` converts errors with From; mixing error types needs a common target.
`Box<dyn Error>` is quick for applications; libraries define an error enum.
A custom error implements Display, Error (with source) and From for each wrapped error.
MAC addresses are 6 bytes; bit 1 of the first byte means local, bit 0 means multicast.
Enums with a loop and match model protocol states and transitions explicitly.

terms.def: A type, usually an enum, that represents the ways an operation can fail.
The Error trait method that returns the lower-level error that caused this one.
A 48-bit hardware address used by Ethernet and Wi-Fi on the local network.
Addressed to a group of devices rather than a single one (unicast).
A model in which a system is in one of a fixed set of states and events cause transitions.
